This repo is a renamed Flask fork (package `tessel`), so the names differ from upstream Flask. Everything is in `src/tessel/views.py`.

**Making it a view function:** `View.to_view_func(cls, name, *class_args, **class_kwargs)` (line 86) is a classmethod that returns a plain function `view(**kwargs)`.
- If `init_every_request` is true, `view` instantiates `view.view_class(*class_args, **class_kwargs)` on each request. Otherwise it reuses one shared instance.
- It then calls `active_app.ensure_sync(self.run_view)(**kwargs)`.
- Any class `decorators` are applied to `view`.
- It copies `view_class`, `__name__`, `__doc__`, `methods` and `provide_automatic_options` onto the function. The route registration (`app.attach_route_rule`) reads `methods` and `provide_automatic_options` from there.

**Routing HTTP methods to handlers:** `VerbView(View)` (line 138) does this in two parts.
- `VerbView.__init_subclass__` (line 165) builds `cls.methods` from any `get`, `post`, etc. defined on the class, using the `http_method_funcs` set (line 11). It also merges in `methods` from base classes, unless the subclass sets `methods` itself.
- `VerbView.run_view` (line 182) does the dispatch with `getattr(self, request.method.lower())`. `HEAD` falls back to `get` if there is no `head` handler. It calls the handler through `active_app.ensure_sync(meth)(**kwargs)`.

So `Foo.to_view_func("foo")` gives a function whose `view` calls `VerbView.run_view`, which calls `Foo.get()` or `Foo.post()` according to `request.method`.
